title: Amazon RDS
content:
RDS Configuration Create a DB subnet group containing two private database subnets in two Availability Zones, then deploy Amazon RDS for MySQL using a Multi-AZ configuration. The database does not use public subnets and is not publicly accessible.
Item Configuration Subnet group Two private database subnets in two AZs. Deployment Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a primary and standby. DB instance class db.t3.small. Storage General Purpose SSD gp3, 20 GiB. Public access No. Security Group sportbooking-rds, allowing 3306 only from sportbooking-app. Database name sport_booking. Master username sportbooking_ad. Endpoint sportbooking-mysql.cudgu8qk8z19.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com. Monitoring Database Insights Standard; Enhanced Monitoring every 60 seconds. Backup Automated backup with a seven-day retention period. Configuration Decisions Select the MySQL engine and Production template. Set the DB identifier to sportbooking-mysql. Select sportbooking-vpc and the private DB subnet group. Select Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Disable public access and attach sportbooking-rds. Create the initial sport_booking database. Verify the following information on the Connectivity & security tab:
Record the endpoint and port 3306 for DB_URL in Secrets Manager. Confirm that Publicly accessible is No. Confirm that the VPC Security Group is sportbooking-rds and accepts connections only from sportbooking-app. Test connectivity from EC2 only after the compute layer is deployed in section 5.5. Schema and data-query results are recorded in section 5.7, so no procedure attempts to use EC2 before EC2 exists.
RDS is configured with Public access: No. The MySQL port 3306 rule accepts traffic only from the sportbooking-app Security Group.
Procedure The RDS procedure starts with the DB subnet group, continues with the private MySQL database, and finishes by verifying the endpoint and Security Group.
Procedure:
Open the DB subnet group workflow
From Amazon RDS, open the database management area and navigate to Subnet groups to prepare a dedicated DB subnet group for the data tier.
Figure 1: Start creating the DB subnet group
RDS requires a DB subnet group to determine which private database subnets can host the database. Initialize the DB subnet group
In Subnet groups, choose Create DB subnet group. This resource must exist before the database so RDS can distribute the two instances across private database subnets in two Availability Zones.
Figure 2: Open the Subnet groups list
Creating the subnet group first makes the prepared private database subnet set available during database creation. Enter DB subnet group details
Enter sportbooking-db-subnet-group as the name, add a description, and select the SportBooking VPC.
Figure 3: Enter DB subnet group details
The subnet group must be in the same VPC as the EC2 application. Selecting another VPC prevents private network connectivity between the application and database. Select Availability Zones and private database subnets
Select the Availability Zones used by the database, select the private database subnets, and choose Create.
Figure 4: Select Availability Zones and private database subnets
Two private database subnets in two AZs provide the network foundation for RDS Multi-AZ and isolate the database from the Internet. Start creating the MySQL database
Choose Create database, select MySQL as the engine, and select the Production template.
Figure 5: Start creating the MySQL database
SportBooking uses MySQL, so Amazon RDS for MySQL provides a suitable managed database and avoids operating a database directly on EC2. Select the template and availability option
Select the Production template, then select Multi-AZ DB instance deployment (2 instances).
Figure 6: Select the template and availability option
This option creates a primary DB instance and an RDS-managed standby in another Availability Zone. Set the database identifier and credentials
Enter sportbooking-mysql as the DB identifier and select Self managed credentials. Enter sportbooking_ad as the master username; the password is concealed in the image.
Figure 7: Set the database identifier and credentials
The DB identifier and credentials are later used to define `DB_URL`, `DB_USERNAME`, and `DB_PASSWORD` in the application secret. Select the DB instance class
Select Burstable classes, then select db.t3.small with 2 vCPUs and 2 GiB of memory.
Figure 8: Select the DB instance class
The `db.t3.small` configuration meets the functional testing scope and establishes a baseline for cost monitoring. Configure storage
Select General Purpose SSD (gp3) and set allocated storage to 20 GiB.
Figure 9: Configure storage
The `20 GiB` allocation supports the data scope of this deployment. Select the RDS network
Select Don’t connect to an EC2 compute resource when configuring Security Groups manually. Select the SportBooking VPC and the private DB subnet group created earlier.
Figure 10: Select the RDS network
Selecting the VPC and subnet group manually ensures that the database remains in private database subnets and prevents unintended security rules from being added. Disable public access and select the Security Group Select Public access: No and select or create the RDS Security Group. Confirm that it allows MySQL 3306 only from the EC2 App Security Group.
Figure 11: Disable public access and select the Security Group
The database has no public access path; only EC2 instances associated with `sportbooking-app` can connect to MySQL. Configure monitoring Select Database Insights - Standard, then enable Enhanced Monitoring with 60-second granularity.
Figure 12: Configure monitoring
Monitoring provides operating-system and database metrics for CPU, connections, and storage. Set the database name and port Open Additional configuration, enter sport_booking as the initial database name, and retain MySQL port 3306.
Figure 13: Set the database name and port
The application requires the `sport_booking` database. If this field is empty or incorrect, the application may connect to the server but not find the expected schema. Configure backups Enable automated backups and set the backup retention period to seven days.
Figure 14: Configure backups
This setting allows RDS to retain automated backups for seven days for recovery. Review cost and create the database Review the estimated monthly cost, public access setting, VPC, Security Group, and storage. Choose Create database.
Figure 15: Review cost and create the database
The final review verifies the instance size, storage, and public-access status before the database is created. Monitor the database status Return to Databases and wait until the status changes to Available.
Figure 16: Monitor the database status
The EC2 application can establish a stable connection only after the database becomes Available. Verify the endpoint and network Open the database and inspect Connectivity & security. Record the endpoint, port, VPC, subnet group, and Security Group.
Figure 17: Verify the endpoint and network
Store the endpoint and port in Secrets Manager. The VPC and Security Group information provides evidence that the database is private and accessible only from the application layer.

title: Application Cleanup
content:
4. Scale In and Delete the Auto Scaling Group The Auto Scaling Group had to be processed before the Launch Template. Reducing capacity to 0 allowed the EC2 instances to terminate in a controlled manner before the scaling configuration was deleted.
Procedure:
Open the capacity settings
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) select sportbooking-asg; and (2) select Edit in Capacity overview.
Figure 1: Open the Auto Scaling Group capacity settings
The ASG is maintaining two healthy EC2 instances. Without reducing capacity, it continues to launch a replacement whenever an instance is terminated. Set capacity to 0
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) set Desired capacity to 0; (2) set Min desired capacity to 0; and (3) select Update.
Figure 2: Set the Auto Scaling Group capacity to 0
Setting both desired and minimum capacity to `0` allows the ASG to terminate every EC2 instance without launching a replacement. Maximum capacity can remain unchanged because the ASG is deleted in a later step. Verify that the ASG has no instances
Refresh the page until the Instances column shows 0. Verify that Desired capacity and the minimum limit are also 0.
Figure 3: Verify that the Auto Scaling Group has scaled down to 0
Delete the ASG only after its EC2 instances have terminated to reduce the risk of leaving an ENI or EBS volume in use. Start deleting the ASG
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open Actions; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 4: Start deleting the Auto Scaling Group
With no remaining instances, the ASG can be deleted without affecting data on a running EC2 instance. Confirm ASG deletion
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) enter delete in the confirmation field; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 5: Confirm Auto Scaling Group deletion
After the ASG is deleted, the Launch Template is no longer referenced by the automatic scaling configuration. After deleting the ASG, also check EC2 > Instances and Elastic Block Store > Volumes. Retain only volumes or snapshots explicitly identified as required backups.
5. Delete the Application Load Balancer The ALB had to be deleted before the Target Group because its listeners referenced the Target Group.
Procedure:
Select and delete the ALB
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open EC2 > Load Balancers and select sportbooking-alb; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete load balancer, then confirm in the displayed dialog.
Figure 6: Select the Application Load Balancer to delete
Deleting the ALB also removes its HTTP and HTTPS listeners and releases the association with the ACM certificate. Wait until the ALB disappears from the list before deleting the Target Group. 6. Delete the Target Group Procedure:
Select the Target Group
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open EC2 > Target Groups and select sportbooking-tg; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete.
Figure 7: Select the Target Group to delete
The Target Group can be deleted only after the ALB and listeners no longer reference it. If AWS reports that the resource is still in use, check for a remaining ALB or listener rule. Confirm Target Group deletion
Verify the name sportbooking-tg, then select Delete.
Figure 8: Confirm Target Group deletion
The target EC2 instances terminated when ASG capacity was reduced to `0`, so the Target Group has no backend to maintain. 7. Delete the Launch Template Procedure:
Select the Launch Template
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open EC2 > Launch Templates and select sportbooking-lt; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete template.
Figure 9: Select the Launch Template to delete
The Launch Template is deleted after the ASG so that no configuration continues to reference the template or any of its versions. Confirm Launch Template deletion
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) enter Delete with the exact capitalization requested on the screen; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 10: Confirm Launch Template deletion
Deleting the template removes every version of `sportbooking-lt` and cannot be undone. 8. Detach Policies and Delete the IAM Role The IAM role was deleted only after all EC2 instances had terminated and no instance profile remained in use.
Procedure:
Select the policies attached to the role
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open the sportbooking-ec2-role role and select every attached policy; and (2) select Remove.
Figure 11: Select the policies to detach from the IAM role
The role shown in the figure has AWS managed policies and the `sportbooking-ec2-policy` customer managed policy attached. These associations must be removed before the role is deleted. Confirm policy removal
Verify the number of selected policies, then select Remove.
Figure 12: Confirm policy removal from the IAM role
AWS managed policies are detached from the role but are not deleted from the AWS account. Select the role to delete
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) return to IAM > Roles and select sportbooking-ec2-role; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 13: Select the IAM role to delete
Select only the project role. Do not delete a service-linked role or a role shared with another resource. Confirm role deletion
Enter sportbooking-ec2-role exactly, then select Delete.
Figure 14: Confirm IAM role deletion
Deleting the role removes the permissions that EC2 used to access S3, Secrets Manager, Systems Manager, and CloudWatch. The sportbooking-ec2-policy customer managed policy remains after it is detached. If the policy is used only by this project, open IAM > Policies, verify that it has no attached entity, and delete the policy together with its non-default versions.

title: Launch Template
content:
Launch Template The Launch Template defines the standard EC2 application configuration: AMI, instance type, IAM instance profile, Security Group, and User Data. EC2 instances run in private application subnets, have no public IP addresses, and accept traffic only from the ALB.
Item Configuration Launch Template sportbooking-lt, version description v1. AMI The validated seed EC2 AMI or an Amazon Linux 2023 AMI with the standardized runtime. Instance type t3.small. IAM instance profile sportbooking-ec2-role. Security Group sportbooking-app, accepting port 8080 only from sportbooking-alb. ASG subnets Private application subnets. Public IP Disabled. User Data Installs the runtime, retrieves the secret, downloads the JAR from S3, and creates a systemd service. User Data used in the Launch Template:
#!/bin/bash set -euxo pipefail APP_DIR="/opt/sportbooking" APP_ARTIFACT_S3_URI="s3://sportbooking-artifacts-3stars-us-east-1/releases/SportBooingSystem-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar" APP_ENV_SECRET_ID="sportbooking/prod/app-env" AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="us-east-1" mkdir -p "$APP_DIR" dnf install -y java-21-amazon-corretto-headless jq awscli || true aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \ --secret-id "$APP_ENV_SECRET_ID" \ --region "$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION" \ --query SecretString \ --output text | jq -r 'to_entries[] | "\(.key)=\(.value)"' > "$APP_DIR/app.env" chmod 600 "$APP_DIR/app.env" aws s3 cp "$APP_ARTIFACT_S3_URI" "$APP_DIR/app.jar" --region "$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION" cat > /etc/systemd/system/sportbooking.service <<'EOF' [Unit] Description=SportBooking Spring Boot Application After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] WorkingDirectory=/opt/sportbooking EnvironmentFile=/opt/sportbooking/app.env Environment=AWS_REGION=us-east-1 Environment=AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 Environment=AWS_S3_REGION=us-east-1 ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -Daws.region=us-east-1 -Daws.s3.region=us-east-1 -Dcloud.aws.region.static=us-east-1 -jar /opt/sportbooking/app.jar Restart=always RestartSec=10 User=root [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target EOF systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable sportbooking systemctl restart sportbooking Verify APP_ARTIFACT_S3_URI, APP_ENV_SECRET_ID, and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION carefully in User Data. An incorrect value in any of these variables allows EC2 to boot but prevents the application service from starting.
Launch Template Procedure Create an AMI from the validated seed instance, then build a Launch Template with the IAM Role, Security Group, and User Data shared by all instances in the Auto Scaling Group.
Procedure:
Create an AMI from the seed instance
Open the prepared seed EC2 instance, then choose Actions > Image and templates > Create image.
Figure 1: Create an AMI from the seed instance
The AMI captures the seed instance state so the Launch Template can create consistent new instances. Name the AMI
Enter a project-specific image name and add a description identifying the SportBooking AMI.
Figure 2: Name the AMI
A descriptive AMI name identifies the image used by SportBooking and its deployment version. Create the image
Review the volume and tags, then choose Create image.
Figure 3: Create the image
This image is the base for ASG instances. An AMI that does not exist or remains pending cannot be used reliably by the Launch Template. Confirm that the AMI was created
Return to EC2 AMIs or the instance page and wait for the successful image-creation message.
Figure 4: Confirm that the AMI was created
Use the AMI only after its state becomes `Available` to prevent ASG launch failures. Start creating the Launch Template
Open EC2 > Launch Templates, then choose Create launch template.
Figure 5: Start creating the Launch Template
The Launch Template standardizes the AMI, instance type, IAM Role, Security Group, and User Data for every EC2 instance in the ASG. Enter the Launch Template name
Enter sportbooking-lt as the Launch Template name and v1 as the version description. Enable the guidance option for EC2 Auto Scaling.
Figure 6: Enter the Launch Template name
The ASG references `sportbooking-lt` and default version `1`. Select the AMI
Open the AMI section and select the AMI created from the seed instance.
Figure 7: Select the AMI for the Launch Template
The AMI ensures that new instances use the same base runtime as the validated environment. Select the instance type
Select t3.small with 2 vCPUs and 2 GiB of memory.
Figure 8: Select the instance type
Compute runs continuously in the ASG. A small instance limits cost while providing sufficient capacity for Spring Boot. Configure the key pair and network security
Select Don’t include in launch template for the key pair, then select the sportbooking-app Security Group.
Figure 9: Configure the key pair and network security
`sportbooking-app` permits port `8080` only from `sportbooking-alb`; public SSH remains closed. Attach the IAM instance profile
Open Advanced details, then select sportbooking-ec2-role as the IAM instance profile.
Figure 10: Attach the IAM instance profile
The role allows EC2 to read the S3 artifact, read Secrets Manager, and register with Session Manager at startup. Enter the User Data bootstrap Paste the User Data script that installs the runtime, retrieves the secret, downloads the JAR from S3, and creates the systemd service. Verify the S3 URI, secret ID, and Region.
Figure 11: Enter the User Data bootstrap
User Data turns the Launch Template into an automated deployment process. Each new instance retrieves its configuration and artifact without manual intervention. Create the Launch Template Review the configuration, then choose Create launch template.

title: Security Groups
content:
Deployment Configuration The three Security Groups sportbooking-alb, sportbooking-app, and sportbooking-rds follow the access chain: users reach the ALB; the ALB forwards traffic to the EC2 application; and the EC2 application connects to Amazon RDS for MySQL.
ALB Security Group Direction Type Port Source/Destination Role Inbound HTTP 80 0.0.0.0/0 Allows HTTP access and redirects it to HTTPS. Inbound HTTPS 443 0.0.0.0/0 Allows HTTPS access. Outbound Custom TCP 8080 EC2 App SG Allows the ALB to forward traffic to the application. Recorded result: the ALB Security Group does not expose ports 8080, 3306, or 22 publicly.
EC2 App Security Group Direction Type Port Source/Destination Role Inbound Custom TCP 8080 ALB Security Group Allows only the ALB to call the application. Inbound SSH Not open Not used Administration uses Session Manager instead of SSH. Outbound HTTPS/All traffic 443/All Internet through NAT or AWS services EC2 must reach S3, Secrets Manager, SSM, and RDS. Recorded result: no 0.0.0.0/0 rule allows inbound access to port 8080.
RDS Security Group Direction/Setting Type Port Source Role Inbound MySQL/Aurora 3306 EC2 App Security Group Allows only the EC2 application to connect to the database. Public access No - - Prevents public Internet access to RDS. Recorded result: RDS accepts connections only from the EC2 App Security Group, not from a public IP address or 0.0.0.0/0.
Post-configuration Verification Record the inbound rules of the ALB, EC2 App, and RDS Security Groups. Verify that the source of the EC2 rule is the ALB Security Group, not a public CIDR. Verify that the source of the RDS rule is the EC2 App Security Group. Do not open public SSH; administer EC2 through Session Manager after attaching the IAM Role. Procedure Create the Security Groups in ALB, EC2 application, and RDS order so every rule references a component that already exists.
Procedure:
Open the Security Groups list
Open EC2 > Security Groups, then choose Create security group.
Figure 1: Open the Security Groups list
A Security Group is a resource-level firewall. Separate Security Groups for the ALB, EC2 application, and RDS support least-privilege access. Configure the ALB Security Group
Enter sportbooking-alb as the name and describe the ALB role. Select sportbooking-vpc, then add inbound HTTP port 80 and HTTPS port 443 rules from 0.0.0.0/0.
Figure 2: Configure inbound rules for the ALB Security Group
Public rules are added only at the ALB layer. Application port `8080` and database port `3306` are not exposed to the Internet. Create the ALB Security Group
Review the outbound rules and Security Group identifiers. Add resource-management tags, then choose Create security group.
Figure 3: Review and create the ALB Security Group
Verify that the Security Group belongs to the correct VPC and contains only the required rules before creating it. Confirm that the Security Group was created
Open the new sportbooking-alb Security Group and inspect the Inbound rules tab and VPC information.
Figure 4: Confirm that the sportbooking-alb Security Group was created
The resource details confirm that `sportbooking-alb` belongs to the correct VPC and has the two HTTP and HTTPS inbound rules. Restrict outbound traffic from the ALB to the application
Open Outbound rules, set the protocol to Custom TCP and the port to 8080. Select sportbooking-app as the destination Security Group, then choose Save rules.
Figure 5: Restrict ALB outbound traffic to port 8080 on sportbooking-app
The ALB can now forward application traffic only to EC2 instances associated with `sportbooking-app` on port `8080`. Repeat the Create security group workflow for the remaining two tiers. sportbooking-app accepts inbound port 8080 only from sportbooking-alb; sportbooking-rds accepts inbound MySQL port 3306 only from sportbooking-app. These three Security Groups are then assigned to the ALB, Launch Template, and RDS respectively.

title: Event 3
content:
Harvest Report: “GameDay - 8 Teams Competing for Glory” Purpose of the Event Create a playground to help participants consolidate and test their knowledge of Amazon Web Services (AWS) through questions and real-world scenarios. Practice the ability to analyze requirements and select appropriate AWS services to solve Cloud architecture problems. Enhance teamwork skills, critical thinking, and decision-making capabilities in a time-constrained environment. Create opportunities for networking, learning, and sharing experiences among students participating in the First Cloud Journey program. Event Information Event name: GameDay - 8 Teams Competing for Glory. Program series: First Cloud Journey. Time: June 20, 2026. Format: Team-based competition with multiple-choice questions and real-world scenarios related to AWS services and architecture. Participants: Students and competing teams belonging to the First Cloud Journey program. Competition Format GameDay was organized as a team-based competition through the Live Match Control system, allowing real-time updates of the leaderboard (Team Scoreboard) and questions. Teams would coordinate to analyze requirements, choose appropriate answers, and compete directly with one another throughout the duration of the contest.
Some highlights of the competition:
Questions were divided into various score levels such as 10 points, 50 points, 100 points, etc., depending on the difficulty. Teams could choose the Minimum Risk mode to reduce risk or use the Hope Star to increase points when confident in their answers. Scores were continuously updated on the leaderboard, creating a lively and highly competitive tournament atmosphere. Teams not only needed to answer correctly but also had to choose appropriate strategies to maximize their scores. Some participating teams included:
Ngũ Đại Hiệp Gặp Phải Thằng Liều Life Long Learner Young Flame IT PrimeOps … Key Highlights The questions in GameDay were built based on real-world system deployment scenarios on AWS. Participants not only needed to memorize the function of each service but also had to analyze requirements, evaluate multiple options, and choose the most suitable solution based on criteria such as performance, security, scalability, and cost.
Security and Access Management on AWS Questions focused on building security systems and controlling access permissions for applications on AWS.
Using AWS WAF with Rate-based Rules to block anomalous requests and mitigate the risk of website attacks. Managing data access permissions on Amazon S3 through Bucket Policies to ensure only authorized entities can access resources. Learning about AWS Artifact to check AWS compliance reports and security certifications for auditing and compliance requirements. Serverless and Automated Data Processing Several questions introduced how to build systems leaning toward Serverless and Event-driven Architecture to reduce operational costs and increase scalability.
Combining Amazon DynamoDB Streams with AWS Lambda to automatically process data when changes occur in the database. Understanding how to build event-driven processing workflows helps reduce manual operations and enhance operational efficiency. Identifying appropriate cases to apply Serverless architecture in practice. Hybrid Cloud and Data Storage Questions required choosing appropriate storage solutions to optimize efficiency and cost.
Using AWS Storage Gateway (File Gateway) to connect on-premises storage systems with AWS. Storing long-term data with Amazon S3 Glacier to reduce costs while still ensuring retrieval capabilities when necessary. Understanding how to deploy a Hybrid Cloud model to combine On-premises infrastructure with the Cloud environment. Databases on AWS The competition also addressed selecting appropriate databases for each type of application.
Using Amazon DynamoDB for applications requiring high performance, flexible scalability, and NoSQL data management. Understanding the advantages of managed databases (Managed Databases) compared to self-deploying and operating them. Knowing how to choose the right database based on the characteristics of each problem. Performance and Scalability Questions helped participants understand how to build systems with flexible scalability that can handle large amounts of traffic.
Using Auto Scaling to automatically adjust the number of resources according to actual traffic. Selecting an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to support Path-based Routing, Host-based Routing, and WebSocket. Designing systems with High Availability and Scalability to meet usage demands. Cost Optimization and AWS Architecture In addition to technical knowledge, GameDay focused on cost optimization and building efficient Cloud architectures.
Using the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate deployment costs before putting the system into operation. Applying the AWS Well-Architected Framework, especially the Performance Efficiency pillar, to choose the right type of resource for each need. Evaluating multiple design options to balance performance, security, scalability, and operational costs. Understanding that each problem can have multiple different solutions, and the choice always depends on the actual requirements of the system. What I Learned Knowledge of AWS Services Through the questions and real-world scenarios in GameDay, I had the opportunity to consolidate and expand my knowledge of many important AWS services.
Better understanding how to use AWS WAF to protect applications against common attacks and control incoming traffic. Grasping how to manage access permissions to Amazon S3 via Bucket Policies to ensure data security. Understanding how to combine Amazon DynamoDB Streams with AWS Lambda to build automated data processing workflows following the Event-driven model. Consolidating knowledge of Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3 Glacier, AWS Storage Gateway, Application Load Balancer, Auto Scaling, AWS Artifact, and the AWS Pricing Calculator. Clearly understanding the role of each service in building a Cloud system with scalability, high availability, and cost optimization. Knowledge of Cloud Architecture Besides learning about individual services, GameDay helped me better understand how to combine AWS services to build a complete architecture.
Understanding how to deploy a Hybrid Cloud model by combining On-premises infrastructure with services on AWS. Grasping how to design systems with scalability, high availability, and good fault tolerance. Understanding the benefits of Serverless and Event-driven architectures in automating data processing workflows. Knowing how to evaluate multiple different deployment options based on criteria such as performance, security, scalability, and cost. System Design Thinking One of the most valuable things I learned after GameDay was the approach to solving an architectural problem on AWS.
There is no single service or architecture that is the best for every case; rather, choices must be made based on the actual requirements of the system. Every design decision requires a trade-off between performance, cost, security, scalability, and availability. Understanding the nature of each service is more important than just memorizing its name or function. Skills Practicing the ability to analyze requirements and select appropriate solutions for each situation. Improving logical thinking and problem-solving skills within limited time. Enhancing teamwork skills, exchanging ideas, and reaching a consensus on solutions with team members. Learning to make decisions based on multiple criteria instead of focusing on a single factor. Application to Work The knowledge and experience gained from GameDay can be directly applied to the learning process as well as real-world projects.
Applying the AWS Well-Architected Framework to evaluate and improve system architecture. Using the AWS Pricing Calculator to budget costs before deploying services on AWS. Selecting appropriate AWS services based on requirements for performance, scalability, security, and cost. Designing scalable systems using Auto Scaling combined with an Application Load Balancer. Building automated data processing workflows using AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB Streams. Applying the learned knowledge into Labs, practical projects, as well as the preparation process for future AWS certifications. Forming an architectural analysis mindset before selecting services instead of solely focusing on technical implementation. Experience During the Event Participating in GameDay - 8 Teams Competing for Glory was a very exciting and rewarding experience. The atmosphere of the competition became lively right from the first questions as teams continuously discussed, analyzed, and submitted answers within the limited time frame. The fact that the leaderboard was updated in real time via the Live Match Control system, along with mechanisms like Minimum Risk and Hope Star, created an attractive competition and required each team to have a suitable strategy for each round of answers.
Experience in Solving Real-World Situations: The questions were all constructed from AWS system deployment scenarios rather than just testing theoretical knowledge. Participants needed to analyze requirements, evaluate multiple options, and choose the most suitable solution for each problem. Many questions had multiple reasonable answers, helping me understand that in reality, a single solution does not always exist. Teamwork and Knowledge Exchange: Team members continuously discussed and shared perspectives before submitting the final answer. The discussion process helped me gain access to many different perspectives in analyzing architecture and selecting AWS services. Observing how other teams solved problems also brought a lot of experience and real-world lessons. Most Impressive Thing: The questions closely followed common scenarios when deploying systems on AWS, helping participants apply their knowledge instead of just memorizing theory. The competition not only evaluated the level of understanding of each AWS service but also required the ability to combine multiple services to build a complete solution. The tactical element in choosing when to use Minimum Risk or Hope Star made the competition more engaging and highly competitive. Lessons Learned: Clearly understanding the nature and purpose of each AWS service is more important than just memorizing the service name. Designing Cloud architecture always needs to balance performance, security, scalability, and cost. Teamwork, exchanging ideas, and analyzing multiple options will help make more accurate decisions. Practicing through real-world scenarios is the most effective way to consolidate and enhance AWS knowledge. Conclusion GameDay - 8 Teams Competing for Glory was not only a competition to test knowledge about AWS services but also an opportunity to apply learned knowledge to real-world situations. Through analyzing requirements, selecting appropriate services, and discussing with team members, I understood more clearly about Cloud architecture design thinking as well as how to evaluate a solution based on multiple factors such as performance, security, scalability, and cost.
The event helped me consolidate my professional knowledge, enhance teamwork skills, and practice problem-solving abilities in a time-pressured environment. This was a meaningful experience, contributing to making me more confident in the process of learning and practicing AWS, as well as preparing for future AWS projects and certifications.

title: Blog 3: How AWS DevOps Agent finds root causes
content:
HOW AWS DEVOPS AGENT USES MULTI-AGENT REASONING TO FIND ROOT CAUSES Confirmation bias is one of the most common reasons incident investigations take longer than necessary. An on-call engineer receives an alert, formulates a hypothesis based on experience, finds a matching piece of evidence, and… stops looking. Meanwhile, the actual root cause — which might lie in another service, a different signal, or a different timeframe — remains unresolved.
Modern distributed systems do not lack telemetry data. What they lack is reasoning capability — the ability to generate multiple explanations simultaneously, actively challenge each hypothesis, and draw conclusions only when supported by definitive evidence.
AWS DevOps Agent, an autonomous agent, solves this problem using a multi-agent architecture. It breaks down incident response processes into specialized capabilities. However, what sets this agent apart is not just its ability to search for data, but its understanding of the architectural context — what resources exist, how they are connected, and how they change after each deployment.
This article dives into the incident investigation lifecycle to explore how the AWS DevOps Agent reasons and transforms from a “black box” into a reliable on-call team member.
1. The Incident Lifecycle AWS DevOps Agent organizes the incident response process into specialized capabilities, mirroring the workflows of top-tier SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) teams. All of these share a common foundation:
Triage: Correlates input signals and enriches the investigation context. Optimized for speed. Investigation: Conducts in-depth root cause analysis with parallel hypothesis generation and validation against counter-evidence. This is the core reasoning engine. Mitigation: Generates immediate remedial actions based on the identified root cause. Prevention: Analyzes patterns from past incidents to prevent future occurrences. All these capabilities rely on one crucial foundation: the Application Topology graph.
2. Topology: The Core Foundation Before it can investigate an incident, the agent needs to understand your architecture — not just as a static list of resources, but as a living map of how they communicate and link back to the source code.
The topology system builds this understanding through:
Analyzing AWS CloudFormation (including AWS CDK). Discovering resources via AWS Resource Explorer. Mapping real-time behavior via CloudWatch Application Signals and third-party platforms (Datadog, Dynatrace). Integrating with CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab) to link to the deployment process. The result is a continuously learning topology structure. When the agent needs to trace an error or assess the blast radius, it relies on this network. Everything operates within an Agent Space — an isolated environment scoped to a specific team or application.
3. Triage: Rapid Categorization and Correlation When an incident occurs (from CloudWatch, PagerDuty, or Grafana), Triage is the first step triggered. It is optimized for rapidly processing large volumes of data in a short time.
The most critical feature of Triage is correlation. The agent automatically links related alarms to determine when they originate from the same event. This minimizes noise and consolidates evidence into a comprehensive investigation. However, ultimate control remains with humans — engineers can easily unlink alerts if they determine they are unrelated.
4. Investigation: The Reasoning Engine This is the centerpiece of the AWS DevOps Agent, following a highly structured methodology.
Context and Data Gathering The agent starts with two questions: What is affected? and What recently changed? It maps the blast radius from the failing resources, checks recent CI/CD deployments, queries metrics and logs from Splunk/Datadog, and analyzes configuration history.
Hypothesis Generation Instead of clinging to a single hypothesis, the agent generates multiple competing hypotheses simultaneously:
Pattern matching: The symptom resembles a past error. Anomaly detection: A previously stable metric suddenly deviates. Temporal correlation: Deployments or resource constraints (CPU, connection pools) coincide with the incident’s onset. Evidence Gathering and Root Cause Determination The agent validates multiple hypotheses in parallel.
Real-world example: The checkout service of an e-commerce site experiences increased latency. The agent formulates 3 hypotheses:
There was a configuration change 20 minutes prior. The payment gateway is responding slowly. The database connection pool is nearing exhaustion. Instead of pursuing just one lead, it checks all three: The configuration change only affected logs (dismissed). The payment gateway slowed down after the checkout latency spiked -> This is a symptom, not the cause (dismissed). The connection pool hit 94% utilization exactly when the errors began -> This is the root cause.
5. Mitigation: Safe by Default After finding the root cause, the agent creates a mitigation plan that includes: A remediation strategy, step-by-step procedures, validation checks, success criteria, and a rollback process.
Key differentiator: The AWS DevOps Agent only creates the plan; it does not automatically execute actions that modify the system. Its “write” permissions are limited to creating tickets. On-call engineers review the plan, assess the impact via the Topology, and make the final decision. This ensures absolute safety when the system is under high stress.
6. Prevention: From Reactive to Proactive The agent’s greatest value lies in connecting the dots between incidents. The Prevention feature groups past incidents that share a common root cause, even if their surface symptoms appear different.
Based on these analyses, the system provides targeted recommendations regarding:
Observability optimization. Testing and validation. Code resilience patterns, such as retry logic or circuit breakers. Infrastructure optimization and governance standards. Engineers can add these recommendations to their backlog or reject them using natural language, allowing the AI to learn for future incidents.
7. Conclusion The AWS DevOps Agent connects these capabilities into a continuous operational flywheel. The Topology graph provides architectural understanding -> Investigation relies on it to trace errors -> Mitigation uses it to assess risks -> Findings feed back into Prevention to stop recurrences.
By recording its entire reasoning process into an immutable journal and preserving operational knowledge even through personnel changes, the AWS DevOps Agent relieves pressure on on-call engineers, helps them make more accurate decisions, and boosts their confidence whenever a midnight incident strikes.

Deployment Scope Build the SportBooking network layer with a VPC, subnets, an Internet Gateway, NAT Gateways, route tables, and Security Groups. Network resources are created before storage, database, and compute resources so later services can use an existing VPC, subnets, and security rules.

content:

Event Information Event name: FCAJ Community Day - “Data Driven, AI Risen”. Program series: First Cloud AI Journey. Time: June 27, 2026. Format: Technical Community Event. Participants: Students, programmers, AI Engineers, Cloud Engineers, DevOps Engineers, and the AWS technology-loving community. Main themes: Generative AI, Multi-Agent Systems, Voice AI, DevOps Automation, Amazon Q, AI Security, and Enterprise AI. List of Speakers Steve Tran - CTO/Founder, CloudThinker. Trung Vu - CEO, Revve AI. Truong Tran - AI Solution Sales, Noventiq. Anh Dang - Solution Sales, Noventiq. Nghi Danh - AI Engineer, Renova Cloud. Kiet Tran - AI Engineer, AWS Student Builder Group. Bao Phan - Cloud Engineer, Cloud Kinetics. Nguyen Nguyen - Cloud Engineer, Cloud Kinetics. Toan Nguyen - AWS Security Builder. Key Highlights FCAJ Community Day focused on bringing Generative AI models from the research phase into practical deployment within enterprises. The program content not only introduced new technologies but also analyzed practical problems concerning performance, security, cost, and operational capabilities when building large-scale AI systems.
Through the sharing sessions, participants had the opportunity to access multiple modern AI architectures such as Multi-Agent, Voice AI, AI Agent for DevOps, Amazon Q, as well as security solutions tailored for the Enterprise environment.
Multi-Agent Architecture and AI Deployment Mindset Steve Tran opened the program by sharing the mindset of developing AI products towards execution rather than merely focusing on theoretical research.
According to the speaker, in startup projects or MVPs, rapidly building products and continuously improving them based on customer feedback will bring far more value compared to spending too much time perfecting the initial design.
Some highlights:
Apply the Champion Customer strategy to collaborate with enterprises to collect real-world data (Ground Truth). Design the system following the Role-based Multi-Agent model, where each AI Agent undertakes a specialized task. Reduce Hallucination by limiting the processing scope of each individual Agent. Focus on optimizing data quality before optimizing the AI model. Through this presentation, I realized that data quality and architectural design play a much more critical role than simply selecting a powerful AI model.
Voice AI and the Vietnamese Language Processing Challenge A very interesting topic of the event was the Voice AI architecture for enterprises.
A complete Voice AI system consists of three main components:
Speech-to-Text. Large Language Model (LLM). Text-to-Speech. To reduce latency, the system utilizes a Streaming Response mechanism, allowing the AI to answer section by section instead of waiting to generate the entire content.
Besides, the speakers also shared the challenges when building Voice AI for the Vietnamese language:
Vietnamese is a low-resource language with limited training data. Difficulty in handling regional intonations and accents. Solving Barge-in situations, where users interrupt while the AI is responding. Through this content, I understand that building Voice AI is not just about integrating a language model but also involves optimizing the entire processing pipeline to deliver a natural communication experience.
AI Agent in DevOps Automation Another topic that garnered significant attention was the application of AI Agents into system operations.
AI is utilized to support the entire incident resolution process, including:
Incident classification. Root Cause Analysis (RCA). Proposing remediation plans. Providing system improvement recommendations. AI Agents are integrated with monitoring platforms such as Dynatrace to analyze topology, logs, and operational history to determine the cause of errors.
In particular, the speaker emphasized the Human-in-the-loop principle, meaning that AI only plays the role of supporting analysis and proposing solutions, while any changes to the Production environment must still be reviewed and approved by humans.
Through this sharing, I better understand the role of AI in modern DevOps, which does not aim to replace operations engineers but helps them make faster and more accurate decisions.
Amazon Q in Corporate Governance The event also introduced how Amazon Q is applied to recruitment and human resource management processes.

title: Auto Scaling Group
content:
Auto Scaling Group The Auto Scaling Group uses the Launch Template to create EC2 application instances in private application subnets and attaches those instances to the Target Group created earlier.
Item Configuration Launch Template sportbooking-lt, version Default (1). Subnets Two private application subnets in two AZs. Desired capacity 2. Min/Max Min 2, Max 4. Target Group sportbooking-tg. Health check EC2 and Elastic Load Balancing; 300-second grace period. Scaling policy Target tracking on Average CPU utilization, target 60, 300-second warmup. Set both desired and minimum capacity to 2 so the ASG maintains two instances across two Availability Zones. Maximum capacity 4 leaves room for the target tracking policy to scale out when average CPU exceeds the target.
Auto Scaling Group Procedure Use the completed Launch Template to deploy instances in private application subnets and register them automatically with the Target Group for health checking.
Procedure:
Start creating the Auto Scaling Group
Open EC2 > Auto Scaling Groups, then choose Create Auto Scaling group.
Figure 1: Start creating the Auto Scaling Group
The ASG maintains EC2 application capacity, replaces unhealthy instances, and supports rollouts through Instance Refresh. Select the Launch Template
Enter sportbooking-asg as the ASG name, select sportbooking-lt as the Launch Template, and select version Default (1).
Figure 2: Select the Launch Template
The ASG creates instances from the Launch Template. An incorrect version can cause instances to use outdated User Data or an outdated AMI. Confirm the template version
Review the AMI, instance type, key pair, and Security Group summary, then choose Next.
Figure 3: Confirm the template version
This is the final template check before the ASG creates instances in private subnets. Select the VPC and private application subnets
Select the SportBooking VPC and private application subnets in multiple AZs.
Figure 4: Select the VPC and private application subnets
EC2 application instances do not need public IP addresses. Private subnet placement ensures that only the ALB can call the application. Configure advanced capacity options
Select Balanced best effort as the distribution strategy, retain Default for Capacity Reservation preference, and choose Next.
Figure 5: Configure advanced capacity options
This deployment prioritizes a simple and stable configuration. A production environment can use mixed instances or Spot Instances to optimize cost. Attach load balancing
Enable load balancer integration, then attach the ASG to the existing sportbooking-tg Target Group.
Figure 6: Attach load balancing
The ASG must register EC2 instances with the Target Group so the ALB can forward traffic and perform health checks. Configure health checks
Enable Elastic Load Balancing health checks, set the health check grace period to 300 seconds, and choose Next.
Figure 7: Configure health checks
A grace period that is too short can cause the ASG to replace an instance before the application finishes starting. Configure group size and scaling limits
Set desired capacity to 2, minimum capacity to 2, and maximum capacity to 4.
Figure 8: Configure group size and scaling
Maintain two baseline instances while allowing the ASG to scale out to four instances. Configure the target tracking policy
Select Target tracking scaling policy, select Average CPU utilization, set the target value to 60, and set instance warmup to 300 seconds.
Figure 9: Configure target tracking for 60% average CPU
This policy adjusts desired capacity between two and four instances based on average CPU utilization across the Auto Scaling Group. Complete the Auto Scaling Group options
Keep deletion protection at None (default) and do not use a placement group. Review monitoring, warmup, and instance-maintenance options, then choose Next.
Figure 10: Review maintenance options and continue
Complete these options before configuring notifications and tags. Skip notifications during ASG creation No notification is added during ASG creation. Choose Next.
Figure 11: Skip or add notifications
The SNS channel is created separately in section 5.7 and used as an action for the CloudWatch alarm. Add an ASG tag Add a tag such as Project=SportBooking, then choose Next.
Figure 12: Add a tag to the ASG
Tags support resource filtering, cost management, and identification of project instances. Review and create the ASG Review the Launch Template, subnets, Target Group, capacity, and tags, then choose Create Auto Scaling group.
Figure 13: Review and create the ASG
Verify the Launch Template, private subnets, Target Group, capacity, and tags before creating the ASG. Verify the ASG after creation Open the new ASG and inspect its instances, desired capacity, Launch Template, and health status.
Figure 14: Verify the ASG after creation
This provides evidence that the compute layer is running and ready to receive traffic through the Target Group and ALB. Instance Refresh Procedure When updating the application version, build the JAR again and overwrite the release object in S3:
.\mvnw.cmd clean package -DskipTests aws s3 cp target\SportBooingSystem-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar ` s3://sportbooking-artifacts-3stars-us-east-1/releases/SportBooingSystem-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar ` --region us-east-1 Then open EC2 > Auto Scaling Groups > sportbooking-asg > Instance refresh > Start and use:
Use current Auto Scaling group configuration. Instance warmup: 300 seconds. Skip matching: Off. Monitor the Target Group until the replacement instances become Healthy. When an empty Launch Template version caused an error, update the ASG to a valid version before restarting the refresh with the current ASG configuration.

title: Data and Access
content:
Deployment Scope Provision the foundational services before deploying EC2: create the S3 buckets and upload the artifact, create the S3 Gateway Endpoint, deploy Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ, create a Secrets Manager secret for application configuration, and then grant the EC2 IAM Role access to the resources that now exist.
Implementation Order Create S3 Buckets, Upload the Artifact, and Configure the Gateway Endpoint Create Private Amazon RDS for MySQL Create the Application Secret in Secrets Manager Create the EC2 IAM Role Create the secret after RDS so DB_URL contains the correct database endpoint. Create the IAM Role after S3 and the secret so its policy can reference ARNs that already exist. Create the Launch Template and EC2 resources only after the artifact, RDS, secret, and role are all ready.
Recorded Results The S3 artifact bucket contains the JAR under the releases/ prefix and is not public. The S3 upload bucket stores football-pitch images and has Block Public Access enabled. The S3 Gateway Endpoint is associated with the route tables of the private application subnets. The sportbooking-ec2-role IAM Role permits SSM access, S3 artifact reads, S3 upload reads and writes, and secret reads. Amazon RDS for MySQL is in private database subnets and is not publicly accessible. The sportbooking/prod/app-env secret contains the configuration required for EC2 to create /opt/sportbooking/app.env.

title: IAM Role
content:
Deployment Scope Create an IAM Role that allows the EC2 application to read the artifact from S3, read and write uploaded files, retrieve configuration from Secrets Manager, and connect through Systems Manager Session Manager. This removes the need to store access keys directly on EC2.
Role Configuration Item Configuration value Trusted entity AWS service: EC2 Role name sportbooking-ec2-role Managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore Inline policy Read the S3 artifact, read/write S3 uploads, and read the secret Attached to EC2 Through the IAM instance profile in the Launch Template Application Inline Policy { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadArtifactJarFromS3", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::sportbooking-artifacts-3stars-us-east-1/releases/*"] }, { "Sid": "AccessUploadFilesInS3", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::sportbooking-uploads-3stars-us-east-1/uploads/*"] }, { "Sid": "ReadAppEnvSecret", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:<account-id>:secret:sportbooking/prod/app-env*"] } ] } Create the IAM Role after the S3 buckets and secret. This allows the custom policy to be checked directly against the artifact bucket, upload bucket, and sportbooking/prod/app-env ARNs before it is attached to the role.
Procedure Start with an EC2 trust relationship, attach the SSM policy, and then attach a policy that limits access to the required S3 and Secrets Manager resources.
Procedure:
Start creating the IAM Role
Open IAM > Roles, then choose Create role.
Figure 1: Start creating the IAM Role
EC2 requires permission to read S3, read Secrets Manager, and use Session Manager without storing access keys on the instance. Select EC2 as the trusted entity
Select AWS service, choose the EC2 use case, and choose Next.
Figure 2: Select EC2 as the trusted entity
The trusted entity determines which service can assume the role. Selecting EC2 allows instances to receive temporary credentials through the instance profile. Find the required managed policy
Search for the SSM policy under Add permissions, then select AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
Figure 3: Find the required managed policy
The SSM policy supports private EC2 administration through Session Manager without opening public SSH. Create the application permissions policy
Open the policy creation workflow or add an inline policy. Enter the JSON permissions for reading the S3 artifact, reading and writing S3 uploads, and reading the secret.
Figure 4: Create the application permissions policy
Grant access only to the SportBooking buckets, prefixes, and secret; do not grant `s3:*` or `secretsmanager:*` across the entire account. Name and create the policy
Enter sportbooking-ec2-app-policy as the policy name, review the permissions, and choose Create policy.
Figure 5: Name and create the policy
A descriptive name makes the policy's purpose clear during an audit. Return to permission selection
Refresh the policy list after creating the new policy, then search for sportbooking-ec2-app-policy.
Figure 6: Return to permission selection
The new policy appears after the list refresh and can be selected for the role. Attach the policies to the role
Select the custom policy, confirm that both the SSM and application policies are selected, and choose Next.
Figure 7: Attach the policies to the role
The role requires both SSM operational permissions and application runtime permissions. Name the role
Enter sportbooking-ec2-role as the role name and add a description of its purpose.
Figure 8: Name the role
This role is selected as the IAM instance profile in the Launch Template and remains separate from roles used by other services. Review and create the role
Verify that the trust policy specifies EC2, review the permission policies, and choose Create role.
Figure 9: Review and create the role
The final review confirms that EC2 is the trusted entity and that the role has both operational and application permissions. Confirm that the role is ready
Find sportbooking-ec2-role in the role list, open it, and verify its permissions.
Figure 10: Confirm that the role is ready
The role is attached to the Launch Template so every EC2 instance in the Auto Scaling Group receives the required permissions at startup.

title: NAT and Endpoint Cleanup
content:
13. Delete the NAT Gateways Both NAT Gateways were deleted before the Elastic IPs and VPC. Each NAT Gateway had to reach Deleted before its Elastic IP was no longer associated.
Procedure:
Select the NAT Gateway in the first Availability Zone
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) select sportbooking-nat-a; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete NAT gateway.
Figure 1: Select the first NAT Gateway to delete
The private EC2 instances have terminated, so Internet access through the NAT Gateway is no longer required. Confirm deletion of the first NAT Gateway
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) enter delete; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 2: Confirm deletion of the first NAT Gateway
The NAT Gateway changes to `Deleting` while AWS processes the request. Select the NAT Gateway in the second Availability Zone
Check the deletion notification for the first NAT Gateway. Then (1) select sportbooking-nat-b; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete NAT gateway.
Figure 3: Select the second NAT Gateway to delete
The architecture uses one NAT Gateway in each of two Availability Zones, so both resources must be removed. Confirm deletion of the second NAT Gateway
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) enter delete; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 4: Confirm deletion of the second NAT Gateway
Deleting both NAT Gateways removes the network resources that otherwise continue to incur hourly charges. Verify the status of both NAT Gateways
Refresh the list until both sportbooking-nat-a and sportbooking-nat-b display Deleted.
Figure 5: Verify that both NAT Gateways have been deleted
Release the Elastic IPs only after NAT Gateway deletion is complete. If attempted too early, the addresses remain associated and cannot be released. Refresh the status periodically and release the Elastic IPs only after both NAT Gateways display Deleted.
14. Release the Elastic IPs Procedure:
Select the Elastic IPs used by the NAT Gateways
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) select sportbooking-eip-us-east-1a and sportbooking-eip-us-east-1b; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Release Elastic IP addresses.
Figure 6: Select the Elastic IPs to release
After the NAT Gateways are deleted, the two Elastic IPs are no longer associated and should be returned to AWS. Confirm release of the Elastic IPs
Verify both IP addresses and Allocation IDs, then select Release.
Figure 7: Confirm release of the Elastic IPs
A released Elastic IP no longer belongs to the AWS account and can be allocated to another account. Verify the Elastic IP list
Confirm the Elastic IP addresses released message, then verify that no project Elastic IP remains in the Region.
Figure 8: Verify that the Elastic IPs have been released
This result confirms that the NAT layer no longer has dedicated public IPv4 addresses allocated. 15. Delete the S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint Procedure:
Select the VPC Endpoint
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) select sportbooking-vpce-s3; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete VPC endpoints.
Figure 9: Select the S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint to delete
The EC2 instances and S3 artifact bucket have been processed, so the endpoint has no remaining traffic to serve. Deleting the endpoint also removes its entries from the associated route tables. Confirm endpoint deletion
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) enter delete; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 10: Confirm S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint deletion
The endpoint is permanently deleted and cannot be restored from its current configuration. Verify that the endpoint has been deleted
Confirm the Successfully deleted endpoints message, then verify that sportbooking-vpce-s3 no longer appears in the list.
Figure 11: Verify that the S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint has been deleted
The VPC no longer contains a custom endpoint that could prevent the final deletion.

title: Troubleshooting
content: Recorded Errors and Resolutions Error Identified cause Resolution JAR upload returns NoSuchBucket The S3 bucket does not exist or the bucket name is incorrect. Create the artifact bucket first and verify the S3 URI. Invalid bucket name <artifact-bucket> The release command still contains a placeholder. Replace the placeholder with sportbooking-artifacts-3stars-us-east-1. RDS missing table The database schema does not contain a table required by Hibernate. Check ddl-auto and application logs, then create the required seed data. S3 Region displays literal ${AWS_REGION} The Region variable was not passed to the application. Add AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, and AWS_S3_REGION=us-east-1. /uploads images return 404 The S3 controller is disabled, the bucket or prefix is incorrect, or IAM permissions are missing. Verify APP_STORAGE_TYPE=s3, the bucket, uploads prefix, and IAM policy. Registration fails on membership levels The membership_levels table has no data. Insert the NONE, SILVER, GOLD, and DIAMOND levels. ACM remains Pending validation The DNS validation CNAME is not public or the domain is misspelled. Verify the hosted zone, registrar name servers, and validation CNAME. Instance Refresh version is empty Desired configuration has no Launch Template version. title: EC2 and Load Balancing
content:
Deployment Scope Deploy the compute layer only after S3 contains the artifact and the IAM Role, RDS, and Secrets Manager resources are ready. The sequence is: create a seed EC2 instance to verify the runtime and permissions; create an AMI and Launch Template; create the Target Group and Application Load Balancer; and finally create the Auto Scaling Group in private application subnets.
Create the Auto Scaling Group after the Target Group and ALB because the ASG is associated with the Target Group during configuration. This order automatically registers and health-checks new EC2 instances as they launch.
Contents Seed EC2 Instance Launch Template Target Group and ALB Auto Scaling Group The pages follow resource dependencies. The seed EC2 instance validates the runtime and access permissions before the AMI is created; the Launch Template is completed before the Auto Scaling Group; and the Target Group and ALB must be ready before the ASG registers instances.

16. Remove Referencing Rules and Delete the Security Groups A Security Group cannot be deleted while it is attached to an ENI or referenced by another Security Group. The ALB, EC2 instances, and RDS database were deleted before this section was performed.
Procedure:
Open the outbound rules of the ALB Security Group
Open the sportbooking-alb Security Group. Select the Outbound rules tab, then select Edit outbound rules.
Figure 1: Open the outbound rules of the ALB Security Group
The outbound rule on port `8080` references the EC2 App Security Group. This reference must be removed before the project Security Groups can be deleted together. Delete the referencing outbound rule
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) select Delete for the port 8080 rule that targets the App Security Group; and (2) select Save rules.
Figure 2: Delete the outbound rule that references the App Security Group
Removing the rule breaks the reference from the ALB Security Group to the App Security Group. Open the inbound rules of the ALB Security Group
Select the Inbound rules tab, then select Edit inbound rules.
Figure 3: Open the inbound rules of the ALB Security Group
The two public HTTP and HTTPS rules were removed to close all inbound access to the Security Group before deletion. Delete the remaining inbound rules
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) delete the HTTPS rule on port 443; (2) delete the HTTP rule on port 80; and (3) select Save rules.
Figure 4: Delete the inbound rules of the ALB Security Group
CIDR-based rules do not create dependencies between Security Groups, but deleting them confirms that the Security Group permits no traffic while cleanup is in progress. Select the project Security Groups
Review and remove any remaining references among sportbooking-app, sportbooking-rds, and sportbooking-alb in the same manner. Then (1) select the three project Security Groups; and (2) open Actions and select Delete security groups.
Figure 5: Select the SportBooking Security Groups
Do not select the `default` Security Group or a Security Group from another VPC. If AWS reports a dependency, check the remaining ENIs and referencing rules before retrying. Confirm Security Group deletion
Verify that the list contains sportbooking-rds, sportbooking-app, and sportbooking-alb. Then (1) enter delete; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 6: Confirm deletion of the Security Groups
Deleting the Security Groups together after removing references prevents unused network configurations from remaining. Verify the result
Confirm the Successfully deleted 3 security groups message, then verify that only default Security Groups or Security Groups from other environments remain.
Figure 7: Verify that the Security Groups have been deleted
This result confirms that the ENIs and Security Group associations of the ALB, EC2 instances, and RDS database have been released. 17. Delete the DB Subnet Group The DB Subnet Group was deleted after RDS because a DB instance using the subnet group prevents its deletion.
Procedure:
Select the DB Subnet Group
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open RDS > Subnet groups and select sportbooking-db-subnet-group; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 8: Select the DB Subnet Group to delete
RDS deletion has completed, so no database continues to reference the subnet group. Confirm DB Subnet Group deletion
Verify the name sportbooking-db-subnet-group, then select Delete.
Figure 9: Confirm DB Subnet Group deletion
This action deletes only the RDS DB Subnet Group configuration; it does not directly delete the VPC subnets. Verify that the DB Subnet Group has been deleted
Confirm the successful deletion message, then verify that only default subnet groups or subnet groups from other environments remain.
Figure 10: Verify that the DB Subnet Group has been deleted
The VPC no longer contains a custom RDS configuration that depends on the private subnets. 18. Delete the VPC The VPC was deleted last, after the compute, database, endpoint, NAT Gateway, and Security Group resources had been processed.
Procedure:
Select the project VPC
On the console, perform the following in order: (1) open VPC > Your VPCs and select sportbooking-vpc; (2) open Actions; and (3) select Delete VPC.
Figure 11: Select the SportBooking VPC to delete
The name, VPC ID, and CIDR were cross-checked to avoid selecting the default VPC or a VPC from another environment. Review dependent resources and confirm
Review the resources that will be deleted with the VPC, including the remaining Internet Gateway, subnets, and route tables. Then (1) enter delete; and (2) select Delete.
Figure 12: Review dependent resources and confirm VPC deletion
The dialog shows `sportbooking-vpc` and 12 related network resources in the deletion request. Every listed resource was verified as belonging to the project. Verify that the VPC has been deleted
Confirm the successfully deleted sportbooking-vpc and 12 other resources message, then verify that only the default VPC or other VPCs that must be retained remain.
Figure 13: Verify that the SportBooking VPC has been deleted
This step completes the cleanup of the SportBooking network infrastructure. If the VPC cannot be deleted, check for remaining ENIs under EC2 > Network Interfaces, VPC Endpoints, NAT Gateways, Load Balancers, RDS resources, cross-referencing Security Groups, and resources managed by other services. Do not delete the default VPC to resolve a dependency error.

title: Workshop
content:
Deploying the SportBooking Football Pitch Booking Website on AWS Website Feature Demo Video Report Scope This report presents the deployment of SportBookingSystem on AWS using a basic production architecture. The website is published through an HTTPS domain; traffic passes through Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer; the Spring Boot application runs on EC2 instances in private subnets; business data is stored in Amazon RDS for MySQL; release artifacts and uploaded images are stored in Amazon S3; and sensitive configuration is managed in AWS Secrets Manager.
The content follows the order in which resources were provisioned: prepare the source code; build the network and security layers; create S3 buckets and upload the artifact; create RDS; store configuration in Secrets Manager; grant IAM permissions; deploy EC2, the ALB, and the Auto Scaling Group; configure DNS and HTTPS; establish monitoring; and finally remove the resources.
The evidence images do not expose database passwords, OAuth client secrets, tokens, access keys, or secret values. The report retains only resource names, Region, status, ports, Security Group sources, and non-sensitive configuration.
Deployment Architecture Component Role Route 53 Manages DNS for sport.younglilliu.id.vn and points an Alias record to the ALB. AWS Certificate Manager Issues the TLS certificate used to enable HTTPS on the ALB. Application Load Balancer Accepts public HTTP/HTTPS traffic, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and forwards requests to the Target Group. Auto Scaling Group + EC2 Runs the Spring Boot JAR in private application subnets and replaces instances during rollouts. Amazon RDS for MySQL Stores application data in private database subnets. Amazon S3 Stores the release JAR and images uploaded through the website. Secrets Manager Stores the database URL, database credentials, domain, S3 configuration, and OAuth configuration. IAM Role + SSM Allows EC2 to read S3 and Secrets Manager and be administered through Session Manager without opening SSH. CloudWatch + SNS Monitors operational status and sends notifications when metrics or alarms cross configured thresholds. CloudFront and AWS WAF Components of the target architecture that were evaluated but were not included in the primary request path for this deployment. Contents Architecture Preparation Network and Security Data and Access EC2 and Load Balancing Domain and HTTPS Operations Cleanup

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Sharing and Feedback Throughout the process of participating in the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program, I had the opportunity to learn, practice, and experience a professional working environment with AWS cloud computing technologies. The program not only helped me enhance my professional knowledge but also trained my working style, self-learning skills, and real-world problem-solving capabilities.
Alongside the positive experiences, I would also like to submit some evaluations and suggestions to contribute to perfecting the program in the future.
I. General Evaluation 1. Learning and Working Environment The learning and practicing environment in the program is very professional, friendly, and highly motivating for interns. The modern workspace at the AWS office (Bitexco Financial Tower) gave me the opportunity to get closer to the corporate environment and actual workflows.
Besides, the program built a positive learning community, where members are always ready to share knowledge and support one another during the learning process as well as project execution.
2. Support from Mentors and the Admin Team This is the point I appreciate the most throughout the program.
The mentors always closely followed the learning process, provided very dedicated guidance, and encouraged interns to find the solutions themselves instead of giving the answers right from the beginning. This helped me form analytical thinking, troubleshooting capabilities, and methods for self-researching technical documentation.
The Admin Team also provided prompt support in allocating AWS Credits, clarifying program regulations, and handling arising issues during the internship.
3. Relevance to the Major of Study The program content is highly practical and well-suited to the orientation of Information Technology students.
During the internship, I had the opportunity to apply the learned knowledge of Java, Spring Boot, databases, and Web application development, while expanding into the AWS cloud computing field through labs and real-world deployment projects.
The combination of foundational knowledge and Cloud technology helped me better understand the process of building and deploying a complete system in a corporate environment.
4. Opportunities for Learning and Skill Development After 12 weeks of internship, I had the opportunity to access and practice with many important AWS services such as:
Amazon EC2 Amazon VPC Amazon RDS Amazon S3 IAM CloudWatch AWS Budgets Auto Scaling Application Load Balancer AWS CLI In addition to professional knowledge, I also significantly improved skills such as:
System architecture design. Requirements analysis and solution building. Cost management on the Cloud platform. Writing technical documentation and Worklogs. Self-learning and researching official documentation. Testing and handling system errors. 5. Culture and Team Spirit One of the highlights of the program is the spirit of knowledge sharing among members.
Although each person executed different contents or projects, everyone was always ready to exchange experiences, support in resolving technical issues, and discuss multiple deployment options together.
This created a positive learning environment, helping each member gain new perspectives when solving problems.
6. Intern Support Policies The program fully provided learning materials, Lab systems, deployment guides, and especially AWS Credits for practice.
Being able to perform Labs in a real AWS environment instead of just learning theory helped me better understand how services operate and gain more practical experience in system deployment.
II. Survey Questions What satisfied you the most during the internship period? What satisfied me the most was experiencing the entire workflow from learning foundational knowledge, practicing AWS Labs, to designing, building, and deploying a real-world project onto the AWS infrastructure by myself.
Through the Online sports field booking system project, I better understood how to combine software development and Cloud infrastructure to build a complete system that is scalable and ready for real-world deployment.
What do you think the program could improve? From my personal perspective, the program has been organized quite methodically with a clear learning roadmap.
However, if there were more direct networking sessions between members, mentors, and professionals working in the industry, it would provide interns with more opportunities to exchange experiences, expand relationships, and learn from real-world situations.
Besides, organizing additional workshops (Workshops) or Tech Talks on system architecture design, cost optimization on AWS, DevOps, and real-world project deployment experiences would give interns more practical insights as well as clearer career orientations.
In addition, if there were periodic Project Review sessions during the project execution phase, mentors would be able to provide early feedback and guidance, helping students timely improve product quality before finalization.
Are you willing to recommend this program to your friends? Yes.
I am completely willing to recommend the First Cloud AI Journey program to students oriented toward the fields of Cloud Computing, Backend, or DevOps.
The program has a clear learning roadmap, rich practical content, and creates conditions for learners to directly access the real AWS environment, thereby accumulating valuable experience for their future careers.
III. Suggestions and Aspirations Suggestions I have a few suggestions to contribute to enhancing the experience for subsequent internship batches:
Organize more specialized Workshops or Seminars on system architecture, DevOps, and cost optimization on AWS. Add periodic Project Review sessions so that mentors can provide early feedback and guidance for each group or individual. Organize more technical exchange activities, Mini Hackathons, or Tech Sharing sessions to strengthen connections among interns and create opportunities to learn from one another. Aspirations After completing the program, I hope to continue accompanying the AWS Study Group and First Cloud AI Journey communities through advanced training programs or knowledge-sharing activities in the future.
At the same time, I hope to have opportunities to participate in larger-scale real-world projects to continue developing my professional knowledge, working skills, and accumulating more experience in the cloud computing field.

title: Cleanup
content:
Cleanup Scope After deployment, testing, and evidence collection were completed, the SportBooking resources were decommissioned in dependency order. The artifact bucket and the compute and network layers were removed. The upload bucket, final RDS snapshot, and retained automated backup were intentionally preserved to protect data required for recovery.
Deleting the Auto Scaling Group, RDS database, S3 bucket, VPC, and IAM role can cause data loss or make the website completely unavailable. Perform these actions only after the required data has been backed up, the report has been completed, and the environment is confirmed to be no longer in use.
Cleanup Order Phase Resources Dependency 1 Route 53, CloudWatch, and SNS Stop directing users to the application; delete the alarm before the SNS topic. 2 ASG, ALB, Target Group, and Launch Template Delete the ASG before the Launch Template; delete the ALB before the Target Group. 3 IAM, RDS, S3, Secrets Manager, and ACM EC2 has stopped; ACM is no longer used by the ALB; no CloudFront distribution was created. 4 NAT Gateway, Elastic IP, and VPC Endpoint Wait until each NAT Gateway reaches Deleted before releasing its Elastic IP. 5 Security Group, DB Subnet Group, and VPC The ALB, EC2 instances, RDS database, endpoint, and Security Group references have been removed. 6 Remaining-resource review No snapshot, backup, log group, hosted zone, or policy remains outside the retention plan. Verify the correct AWS account and Region us-east-1 before every action. Select only resources named for the SportBooking project; do not delete default or shared resources.
Preparation Before Deletion Identify the final RDS snapshot, retained automated backup, and data in the upload bucket that must be preserved. Stop the Alias record sport.younglilliu.id.vn from routing to the ALB before deleting the load-balancing layer. Confirm that no CloudFront distribution was created, so no CloudFront dependency needs to be removed. Retain the public hosted zone because the domain remains managed; remove only records that are no longer used. Record every retained storage resource so that it is not mistaken for an overlooked resource.
